title: Lines of Fit
short: Draw a line close to the points and use its equation to predict.
trouble: Students draw a line through the first and last points instead of following the overall trend.

blocks.html: When the points in a scatter plot cluster around a line, one line can sum up the trend. You can write its equation in slope-intercept form and use it to predict.

A line of fit trades many points for one simple rule. Its slope gives the typical change in $y$ for each 1 more in $x$, and its intercept gives a starting value. Because it is drawn to follow all the points, with some above and some below, it describes the trend better than a line through any two particular points.

Draw a line that follows the trend, with about as many points above it as below. Pick two points on the line (they don’t have to be data points), find its equation, and use it to predict. The slope is the average change per unit; the intercept is the predicted value at $x = 0$.

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: Drag the two handles of your line to fit the points. Then turn on the best-fit line to compare.

blocks.title: Write the equation
blocks.q: A line of fit for the study data passes through $(2, 56)$ and $(7, 81)$. Write its equation.

blocks.title: Predict
blocks.q: Use $y = 5x + 46$ to predict the score of a student who studies 5 hours.
steps: It is a prediction from the trend; a real student could score a bit higher or lower.

blocks.title: Interpret
blocks.q: What do the 5 and the 46 in $y = 5x + 46$ mean?
steps: Slope 5: each extra hour of study goes with about 5 more points, on average.
Intercept 46: the predicted score with 0 hours of study.
blocks.a: about 5 points per hour; a starting value of 46

blocks.html: Drawing the line through the first and last points. Those two points might be unusual, and the line can end up above or below most of the others. Look at the whole cloud, and balance the points above and below the line.
